Puzzle 1 · 2 of 11

The tree Compose remembers

Every composable call records a group through the Composer, and then returns. Here's where those records go, so that a counter's value survives the call that made it, and the same call finds it again next time.

  • Puzzle 0: What @Composable really does

    The Compose compiler plugin rewrites every @Composable function. It adds a hidden $composer parameter (and a $changed one), and wraps the body in a start and an end, so everything the call records in between forms its group. The group's key comes from the function's name and parameters, so every call to the same function opens a group with the same key. Each composable passes its Composer on to the composables it calls, which is why only a composable can call a composable.

The problem

Puzzle 0 showed every composable call recording a group through the Composer, and then returning. When a function returns, its local variables are gone. So where does remember { mutableStateOf(0) } keep that 0 between runs? And puzzle 0 said every call to Counter opens a group with the same key. When Counter runs again, how does it find its own 0, and not the one from another Counter on the same screen?

See it

The building block

The first time your composables run, the Composer builds the composition: a tree of groups, one per call, nested the way the calls nest. Android's docs put it in one line: "A Composition is a tree-structure of the composables that describe your UI." Unlike the calls, it stays: from then on it's only updated, by recomposition.

Some calls leave more than a group. Text, Button, Column: the composables that end up on screen also leave a node, a real UI element with a size and a place on screen. In Compose's UI library the node class is LayoutNode ("an element in the layout hierarchy"). Your own Greeting and Counter leave only groups: they arrange calls, they aren't elements. So the nodes, taken out of the groups, form a smaller tree of their own: the UI tree, which puzzle 5 turns into pixels.

Groups also keep values, in slots. A slot holds an argument the call got last time (puzzle 4 compares against it) or a value it asked to keep. That's all remember is: in the runtime's own code, remember { … } is a call that asks the current Composer to store the value in the composition, at this group. It doesn't become a global: two Counters are two groups, with two slots and two counts.

The runtime keeps the whole composition in one structure, the slot table: each group with its key, followed by its slots and then its children, laid out in the order the calls ran. Reading it from start to end is fast; jumping around in it is not.

So the next run reads it from the start, in step with the calls. Each call arrives with its function's key (puzzle 0) and takes the group with that key at the reader's position: Column finds the Column group, then Counter finds the next group, the one with Counter's key, and its slots, with the 0 in them. Two Counters side by side carry the same key, so their order tells them apart: the first call gets the first group. Android's docs say it the same way: Compose "uses the execution order" to keep instances apart.

What about a call that only runs sometimes? Put a call to ErrorBanner() inside an if on showError, above Counter(). The plugin gives the if a group of its own, keyed by where the if sits in your source (a key from position, as puzzle 0 said), and records that group on every run: empty while showError is false, holding ErrorBanner's group when it's true. So the group after it is always Counter's, and Counter keeps its count. The runtime's code calls these groups for control flow, "such as an if statement", replace groups: when the content changes, the old content is removed and the new one inserted.

One case order can't solve, a loop that calls the same composable for every item, is puzzle 2.

Go deeperWhat does the slot table look like in memory?
Why does the runtime store groups in call order in arrays, instead of as a tree of objects that point at each other?

The next run reads the groups in the same order the calls happen, and a front-to-back scan of an array is fast. The default table is two arrays (one for groups, one for slots) with a gap kept where the next insert goes, so adding a group there, like ErrorBanner's, doesn't shift everything after it. A linked-list version, faster for moving and deleting content, is being tried behind a flag that's off by default.

Back to the main puzzle

The analogy

The stage manager's prompt book from puzzle 0. The first performance fills it in, scene after scene, with each scene's notes inside it (its group). On some pages there's a set piece that goes on stage (a node). Margins hold what to keep: which hat the hero wore (slots). The next night, the stage manager turns the pages in order as the scenes come, so the hero's scene opens at the same page and finds the same hat. A scene that's only sometimes played still has its own page, blank on the nights it isn't played, so the pages after it never move.

Check yourself

Above Counter(), whose count is 3, the code calls ErrorBanner() only if showError is true. showError was false, becomes true, and the screen runs again. What's Counter's count now?

Not quite. ErrorBanner's group is new, inside the if's group; Counter's group and slots stay Counter's.

Not quite. The if's group was there even while showError was false; Counter's group never moved a place.

Right. The if keeps a group of its own, so nothing after it shifts.

A screen calls Counter() twice, one under the other, each with remember { mutableStateOf(0) }. You tap the second one twice, and the screen runs again. What does each remember hand back?

Not quite. The counts aren't locals: they sit in slots of each call's group, which stay after the calls return. Re-read that part ↑

Not quite. remember stores the value in a slot of this call's group; two calls, two groups, two slots.

Right. Each call finds its own group by order, and its own slot inside it.

Both Counter calls on that screen open groups with the same key. Why can't the next run find each one's group by its key alone?

Right. Same function, same key: order decides.

Not quite. Each group's slots come right after it in the table, so finding the group finds its slots.

Not quite. The plugin computes keys while compiling, and the table keeps each group's key.

  • Android Developers: Lifecycle of composables ("A Composition is a tree-structure of the composables that describe your UI."; "A Composition can only be produced by an initial composition and updated by recomposition."; "Even though LoginInput went from being called first to being called second, the LoginInput instance will be preserved across recompositions."; "Compose uses the execution order in addition to the call site to keep the instance distinct in the Composition.")
  • Android Developers: State and Jetpack Compose ("A value computed by remember is stored in the Composition during initial composition, and the stored value is returned during recomposition.")
  • Compose runtime source: Composables.kt (remember is "currentComposer.cache(false, calculation)"; and in Composer.kt, cache's comment: "Cache, that is remember, a value in the composition data of a composition.")
  • Compose runtime source: Composer.kt ("Start a replace group. A replace group is a group that cannot be moved during must only either be inserted, removed, or replaced. For example, the group created by most control flow constructs such as an if statement are replaceable groups.")
  • Compose compiler plugin source: ComposableFunctionBodyTransformer.kt (in visitWhen, an if with one branch that calls composables becomes a coalescable group; "if a call happens after the coalescable child group, then we should realize the group of the coalescable child", and realizing it wraps the whole if in "irStartReplaceGroup(this, scope, …)" and "irEndReplaceGroup(…)", keyed by sourceKey(), its position in the function)
  • Compose runtime source: SlotTable.kt ("Groups form a tree where the child groups are immediately after the group fields for the group. This data structure favors a linear scan of the children. Random access is expensive unless it is through a group anchor."; "Slots are allocated in the slots array and are stored in order of their respective groups."; a node is "where the LayoutNode is stored by the slot table")
  • Compose runtime source: ComposeRuntimeFlags.kt ("A feature flag than can be used to enable the link-list based slot table implementation instead of the gap buffer based slot table."; "This flag is disabled by default.")
  • Compose UI source: LayoutNode.kt ("An element in the layout hierarchy, built with compose UI.")

What you now know

The first run of your composables builds the composition, a tree of groups, one per call, nested the way the calls nest, and kept after they return. Composables such as Text and Button also leave a node, a real UI element. Groups keep values in slots, and the runtime stores all of it in call order in the slot table. The next run walks the table in the same order, matching each call to the group with its key at that point; an if keeps a group of its own, so a call that only sometimes runs doesn't shift the ones after it.
